how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Pressure washing bid calculator

How much should I charge for pressure washing?

A flat price per square foot treats a driveway and a house soft wash as the same surface. They aren't: a clean concrete driveway runs around 1,000 sq ft/hour, a house soft wash closer to 500, a wood deck around 350, a roof around 250. And a $200 driveway around the corner is not the same job as a $200 driveway 40 minutes away — travel and setup are billed hours too, and a long drive each way can cut the after-travel hourly in half.

Open the free pressure washing bid calculator

What a flat $/sq ft price cannot see

Surface mix. Driveway, siding, deck, and roof each wash at a different production rate. Blending them into one number underbids whichever surface is slowest.

Drive time. Travel and setup are hours you're not washing anything, and they're the same billed time as the job itself.

The minimum. A job priced only by square footage can come in under what it costs just to show up, load the rig, and drive there.

A bid you can defend

  1. Split the job by surface and divide each by its own production rate (sq ft/hour).
  2. Add drive time and setup as their own hours.
  3. Add chemical cost and a minimum job floor.
  4. Load the wage, then add overhead, and price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin).

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser and reports the after-travel hourly rate — the number a flat per-foot price hides. Production rates are ballpark starting points, not a guarantee for your equipment or soil conditions; time your own crew and replace them.

Worked example

A $200 driveway wash takes about the same on-site time whether it's around the corner or 40 minutes away — but the second job adds 80 minutes of round-trip driving that the first one doesn't. Priced only per square foot, both look identical. Priced with drive time included, the after-travel hourly on the far job can be roughly half of the near one. The calculator reports that number before the quote goes out, not after the day is already booked.

Common questions

How do I price a pressure washing job?

Split the job by surface (driveway, house siding, deck, fence), divide each by a production rate in square feet per hour, add drive time and setup, then load wage, chemicals, overhead, and margin. A flat price per square foot cannot see that house siding washes much slower than a driveway, or that a 40-minute drive each way can cut the after-travel hourly in half.

Why is my pressure washing bid unprofitable even when the per-foot price looks fine?

Travel and setup are billed hours. A $200 driveway with 80 minutes of driving is a different job from a $200 driveway around the corner. This calculator reports the after-travel hourly so the drive is visible before the quote goes out.

What is a typical pressure washing production rate?

Ballpark starting points only: about 1,000 sq ft/hour for a clean concrete driveway, 500 for a house soft wash, 350 for a wood deck, 250 for a roof. Real rates depend on equipment, soil, storey height, and hand work. Time your own crew and replace the starting figures.

No warranty. This free page is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, chemical, and travel costs, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. vs-a-flat-10-cents-a-square-foot-price.h.text:
← Pressure Washing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat 10¢ a square foot price

“Ten cents a square foot” is not a price for a wash job — it is a price for one surface, quietly reused the moment the customer asks to add the siding while the crew is already there.

What a flat price per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote a wash: multiply the total area by a number and read off a price. It is the number a homeowner holding a mailbox flyer or a search-result special will call and ask you to match, whatever surfaces their job actually adds up to.

The number behind it was set for one surface — usually the concrete driveway advertised on the flyer — and then reused for whatever else gets folded into the square footage, whether or not the rest of the job washes anywhere near as fast as concrete does.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each surface — driveway, walkway, siding, fence, roof — with its own square footage and production rate, plus your loaded wage, round-trip drive, setup, water, overhead, and target margin. It prices each surface's hours separately, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this job's actual surface mix, not a generic one.

What a flat price per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether the job is all concrete driveway or mostly siding, even though siding washes at roughly half the driveway's production rate. Prices each surface at its own production rate, so a siding-heavy job costs more per square foot than a driveway-only job of the same area.
Has no line for round-trip drive time or setup, so a rate that happened to clear cost on the job it was fit to can fall short the moment the surface mix changes. Prices drive time and setup as billed hours on every job, and reports the after-travel hourly rate that number works out to.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-square-foot rate, so an add-on job can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two jobs, the same surface-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped starting rates ($22/hr wage, 25% burden, 40-minute round-trip drive, 20-minute setup, $8 water, $15 equipment wear, 15% overhead, a 25% target margin, $175 minimum):

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $0.1039/sq ft rateGap
2,000 sq ft concrete driveway, no other surfaces — the job the rate is set from$207.77 bid price; $155.82 break-even cost$207.77 (exactly $0.1039/sq ft — this rate is fit to this job)No gap on the job the rate was built on.
2,700 sq ft job: a 300 sq ft driveway plus 2,400 sq ft of soft-washed siding — 94% of the wash hours — added while the crew is already on-site$372.98 bid price; $279.74 break-even cost$280.48The rate clears this job's own break-even cost by just $0.75 — a 0.3% margin instead of the 25% targeted — and quotes $92.50 below the calculator's own bid price.

The $0.1039/sq ft rate is not invented — it is this calculator's own price on the driveway-only job, divided by that job's own square footage. It fits that one job by construction. Applied to the siding-heavy add-on job, it still charges by total square footage and never sees that siding is washing at half the driveway's rate. Run your own job's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-square-foot rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one surface mix it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per square foot get a pressure-washing bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is which surfaces are on the job, not the total square footage a homeowner adds up. Concrete washes at roughly 1,000 sq ft an hour with a surface cleaner; soft-washed siding runs closer to 500 sq ft an hour. A flat rate set from a driveway call cannot see that the siding added once the crew is already on-site takes twice the hours per square foot.

What does a flat price per square foot usually leave out entirely?

Which surfaces make up the total. A rate fit to a fast-washing surface like a concrete driveway is quietly reused for slow-washing surfaces like siding, fencing, or a roof, none of which show up separately once everything is folded into one square-footage number.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting rates: a 2,000 sq ft driveway alone bids at $207.77, or $0.1039 a square foot. Applying that same rate to a 2,700 sq ft job that is mostly a 2,400 sq ft siding wash (94% of the wash hours) prices at $280.48 — just $0.75 above that job's own $279.74 break-even cost, a 0.3% margin instead of the 25% targeted, and $92.50 below the calculator's own $372.98 bid.

Is a flat price per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — the same surface mix as the job the rate was set from — a per-square-foot rate can land close, and on this calculator's own driveway-only preset it is exactly the rate that job supports, because it was set from that job. The risk is applying the same rate once the surface mix changes, because the rate does not know how much siding, fencing, or roof is on the next job and neither does the estimator until the surfaces are actually split out.

Does this calculator know what labor or chemicals cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor, chemical, or water rates. It takes each surface's square footage and production rate, your wage, burden, drive time, setup, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job — the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

← Pressure Washing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. GorillaDesk

Two different shapes: GorillaDesk is an account-based platform for running a pressure-washing (or lawn-care, or pest-control) company's whole operation, including scheduling and invoicing a job once it is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this wash job cost, before you offer it to the customer.

What each tool is for

GorillaDesk is a field-service management platform marketed to pressure washing, lawn care, pest control and other route-based service businesses. It is used to run CRM and customer records, scheduling and route planning, invoicing and payments, and a mobile app for technicians in the field, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. GorillaDesk's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that scheduling and invoicing software describe running and billing a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a new wash job should cost from surface square footage, a production rate, chemical cost and drive time before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what GorillaDesk does. It does not store a customer record, plan a route across a season, or invoice anyone. It takes one job's surfaces — each one's square footage and the production rate your crew actually hits — plus chemical cost, round-trip drive, setup, loaded technician wage, water, overhead, target margin and a minimum job, and turns that into the bid price, the price per square foot, the after-travel hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
